entry: Persian poetic work on Sufism by Rumi. The *Masnavi* (title meaning "The Spiritual Couplets") is a series of six books of poetry totaling around 25,000 verses, and it is one of the most influential works in the history of Sufism. Rumi began dictating it around 1258, at the request of his disciple Husam al-Din Chalabi, and kept composing until his death in 1273; the sixth book remains incomplete. Built from stories and anecdotes drawn from the [[Quran|Quran]], [[Hadith|hadith]] and everyday tales, it teaches Sufi disciples how to reach their goal of being truly in love with God. Some Muslims regard it as the most important work of Islamic literature after the Quran, and many commentators have called it the greatest mystical poem in world literature.

Physical principle that mass and energy are equivalent in a system's rest frame, expressed as E = mc². In the formula, E is the energy of a particle at rest, m is its mass and c is the [[Speed of light|speed of light]], so a small amount of mass corresponds to an enormous amount of energy. The principle arose from [[Special relativity|special relativity]] as a paradox described by the French polymath [[Henri Poincaré|Henri Poincaré]]. [[Albert Einstein|Einstein]] was the first to propose it as a general principle, in a paper on the inertia of bodies published in 1905. When mass is lost in a nuclear or chemical reaction, a corresponding amount of energy is released as light or heat, a principle fundamental to nuclear and particle physics.

Setting of the Mass ordinary by [[Johann Sebastian Bach|Johann Sebastian Bach]] (BWV 232). Completed in 1749, the year before Bach's death, it was built largely on earlier work, including a Sanctus he had composed in 1724. Most Lutheran masses of the period consisted only of a Kyrie and Gloria, but this is a *Missa tota* that sets every part of the Catholic Mass to music. It is scored for five soloists, a five-part choir and a Baroque ensemble with brass and wind instruments, and it lasts around two hours. Bach began the Kyrie and Gloria in 1733 and presented them to Augustus III in [[Dresden|Dresden]], hoping for a court title. Its earliest documented complete performance took place in 1859. Bach's manuscript was included in the [[UNESCO|UNESCO]] Memory of the World International Register in 2015, and the work is now among Bach's most popular vocal works.

Manufacturing of standardized products in a constant flow, especially on assembly lines. It is one of three main production methods, along with job production and batch production. The term was popularized by a 1926 article in the [[Encyclopædia Britannica|Encyclopædia Britannica]] supplement, written from correspondence with [[Ford Motor Company|Ford Motor Company]]. Some techniques, such as standardized sizes and production lines, predate the [[Industrial Revolution|Industrial Revolution]] by centuries, but modern mass production became possible only in the mid-19th century, when machine tools and [[Interchangeable parts|interchangeable parts]] were developed. Its core principle is that the skill is built into the tool, so the worker need not be highly skilled. The approach is capital- and energy-intensive, and the machinery for a line, such as robots and machine presses, is expensive, so a product must be assured of success. It is applied to bulk fluids and minerals as well as to clothing, textiles and automobiles.

Spread of illness symptoms through a cohesive group with no infectious agent or known organic cause. Also called mass hysteria or epidemic hysteria, it originates from a [[Nervous system|nervous system]] disturbance and is distinct from collective [[Delusion|delusions]] because its symptoms are physical. Outbreaks often affect schoolchildren or workers in enclosed settings, frequently involving adolescents and females, and the symptoms are typically transient and benign. Intense media coverage tends to worsen outbreaks. They usually resolve once the group is separated and reassured by authorities.

Analytical technique that measures the mass-to-charge ratio of [[Ion|ions]]. Results are displayed as a mass spectrum, a plot of intensity against mass-to-charge ratio. Spectra reveal the elemental or [[Isotope|isotopic]] signature of a sample, the masses of particles and molecules, and the chemical structure of compounds. A sample, which may be solid, liquid or gaseous, is [[Ionization|ionized]], for example by bombardment with electrons, and the resulting ions are accelerated, separated by electric or magnetic fields, and detected. In 1899, Wilhelm Wien built a device that separated positive rays by charge-to-mass ratio, and [[J. J. Thomson|J. J. Thomson]] later refined the method. Ernest O. Lawrence's calutrons, a type of sector mass spectrometer, separated uranium isotopes during the [[Manhattan Project|Manhattan Project]]. In 1989, half of the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for the ion trap technique.

U.S. state in the [[New England|New England]] region of the Northeastern United States (pop., 2024: 7,136,171). Its capital and largest city is [[Boston|Boston]]. Massachusetts was an early site of English colonization, and the [[American Revolution|American Revolution]] originated there. Originally dependent on agriculture, fishing and trade, it became a manufacturing hub during the [[Industrial Revolution|Industrial Revolution]]. Its economy shifted to services in the 20th century, and in the 21st century it became a global leader in [[Biotechnology|biotechnology]]. It is home to [[Harvard University|Harvard University]] and the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], and it was the first U.S. state to legally recognize [[Same-sex marriage|same-sex marriage]].

Private research university in [[Cambridge, Massachusetts|Cambridge, Massachusetts]], United States. Founded by geologist William Barton Rogers to accelerate American industrialization through scientific knowledge, it adopted a German polytechnic model emphasizing laboratory instruction in applied science and engineering. Its first classes were held in Boston in 1865, and it moved to its current Cambridge campus in 1916. During World War II, its Radiation Laboratory made the institute the nation's largest non-industrial research and development contractor, and graduate enrollment and research funding grew rapidly in the postwar decades. It became closely associated with [[Computer science|computer science]], [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] and [[Biotechnology|biotechnology]], although engineering remains its largest school. Tuition is generally not charged to undergraduates from families with incomes below $200,000.

English trip hop group formed in [[Bristol|Bristol]] in 1988. Its debut album, *Blue Lines* (1991), is generally considered the first trip-hop album. The single "Unfinished Sympathy" reached number one on the Dutch Top 40. *Mezzanine* (1998) gave the group their first number one on the UK Albums Chart. Robert "3D" Del Naja and Grant "Daddy G" Marshall have continued as a duo since Andrew "Mushroom" Vowles left in 1999. The group's five studio albums have sold over 13 million copies worldwide. Its awards include a Brit Award for Best British Dance Act, and it supports political, [[Human rights|human rights]] and environmental causes.

Postgraduate academic degree demonstrating mastery of a specific field or area of professional practice. A master's degree normally requires previous study at the [[Bachelor's degree|bachelor's]] level, either as a separate degree or as part of an integrated course. Graduates are expected to have advanced knowledge of a specialized body of theoretical and applied topics, along with high-order skills in analysis, critical evaluation or professional application. The degree descends from the medieval *licentia docendi*, or license to teach. In the United States, the first master's degrees were awarded at [[Harvard University|Harvard University]] soon after its foundation. In 2023, approximately 25.3 million Americans held one, representing about 11% of adults aged 25 and older. Holders earn a median weekly wage of $1,840, compared with $1,543 for bachelor's recipients.

Large, powerful type of [[Dog|dog]]. Mastiffs are among the largest dogs, with a short coat, a long low-set tail, large feet, a large bulky skull, a broad short muzzle and drooping ears. Records of mastiff-type dogs in Europe and Asia date back 3,000 years. Mastiffs have historically been guard dogs that protected homes and property, but they were also used for hunting, war and blood sports such as bull-baiting and bear-baiting. Although often grouped with livestock guardian dogs, mastiffs form separate genetic populations. Older English sources call them bandogs. The English Mastiff, a classic breed, is docile and dignified, aloof with strangers but loyal to its family. The American Kennel Club recognized the breed in 1885.

Extinct proboscidean genus, *Mammut*, endemic to North America. Mastodons lived from the late [[Miocene|Miocene]] to the early [[Holocene|Holocene]] and belong to the same order as [[Elephant|elephants]] and [[Mammoth|mammoths]], although they had stockier builds and lower-domed skulls. The best-known species, *Mammut americanum*, is thought to have stood 275–305 cm at the shoulder. Mastodons browsed on leaves and woody plants, with females and juveniles living in herds and adult males living largely solitary lives. [[Clovis culture|Clovis culture]] and other Paleoindians hunted them. Mastodons disappeared in the end-[[Pleistocene|Pleistocene]] extinction event, which also eliminated most of North America's largest animals.

Form of autoeroticism in which a person sexually stimulates one's own genitals, usually to [[Orgasm|orgasm]]. It is frequent in both sexes, and clinicians consider it a healthy, normal part of sexual enjoyment. Techniques include touching by hand, using everyday objects or [[Vibrator (sex toy)|vibrators]], and it may also be performed with a partner, known as mutual masturbation. Religions vary in their views. In the 18th and 19th centuries, some European theologians and physicians described it in negative terms, but such taboos generally declined in the 20th century. The word was introduced in the 18th century, based on the Latin verb *masturbari*. Its legal status has varied, and masturbation in public is illegal in most countries. It has been observed in many non-human animals.

Dutch exotic dancer and courtesan. Born Margaretha Geertruida Zelle in Leeuwarden, the Netherlands, she married Dutch colonial army captain Rudolf MacLeod and lived with him on [[Java|Java]] in the [[Dutch East Indies|Dutch East Indies]]. Her stage name means "sun" in Indonesian. She was convicted of being a [[Espionage|spy]] for Germany during [[World War I|World War I]] and was executed by firing squad in France. Later biographers argue that the French Army needed a scapegoat and that the files used against her contained falsifications, and some argue that she could not have been a spy. Her story made her name synonymous with the femme fatale.

Philosophical doctrine that matter is the fundamental substance of nature. Materialism is a form of [[Monism|monism]] holding that all things, including mind and [[Consciousness|consciousness]], arise from material interactions and depend on physical processes. It contrasts with [[Idealism|idealism]], which treats consciousness as fundamental, and it is closely related to [[Naturalism (philosophy)|naturalism]] and to physicalism, which extends matter to include energy, forces and spacetime. Ancient atomists such as [[Democritus|Democritus]] and [[Epicurus|Epicurus]] explained all change through the motion of atoms, and [[Thomas Hobbes|Thomas Hobbes]] advanced materialism in the modern era. A central controversy is the hard problem of consciousness: critics argue that material accounts fail to capture subjective experience, while proponents hold that it emerges from complex neural configurations.

Interdisciplinary field concerned with the structure of materials, their properties, and how to design them for specific applications. The internal structure of a material, from atomic arrangements to microscopic features, strongly influences its mechanical, electrical, thermal and optical behavior. Practitioners use the processing–structure–properties–performance paradigm, in which processing determines structure, structure determines properties, and properties control performance in service. The field grew out of [[Metallurgy|metallurgy]] and ceramics, among the oldest forms of engineering, and drew on chemistry, physics and engineering from the [[Age of Enlightenment|Enlightenment]] onward. It was widely recognized as a distinct field only from the 1940s. In the late 19th century, [[Josiah Willard Gibbs|Josiah Willard Gibbs]] showed that the thermodynamic properties of atomic phases relate to the physical properties of materials. Work for the [[Space Race|Space Race]] advanced metal alloys and silica and carbon materials. The field has contributed to biomaterials, [[Nanotechnology|nanotechnology]] and [[Semiconductor|semiconductors]].

Number whose value is fixed by an unambiguous definition and often given a special symbol or name. Constants such as [[Pi|π]] and e occur in geometry, number theory, statistics and [[Calculus|calculus]]. Some arise from a fundamental principle, as π does, while others are notable mainly for historical reasons. The square root of 2, known as Pythagoras' constant, is the length of a diagonal across a unit square and is an [[Irrational number|irrational number]]. π is irrational and transcendental, and it appears in many formulas in physics as well as in pure mathematics. Euler's number e, the base of the [[Exponential function|exponential function]], was discovered by [[Jacob Bernoulli|Jacob Bernoulli]] to arise in compound interest. All named mathematical constants are definable numbers, and usually computable.

Method of proof showing that a statement holds for every natural number. The proof has two parts. The base case establishes the statement for the first case, usually n = 0 or n = 1, and the induction step shows that if it holds for n = k, it also holds for n = k + 1. The idea is often illustrated by falling dominoes or climbing a ladder. Mathematical induction is an inference rule in formal proofs and the foundation of most correctness proofs for computer programs. It extends to well-founded structures such as trees, a generalization known as structural induction that is closely related to [[Recursion|recursion]]. Despite its name, it differs from [[Inductive reasoning|inductive reasoning]] in philosophy, because it gives a rigorous proof by a finite chain of deductive reasoning rather than a probable conclusion. Al-Karaji used an implicit form of the argument around 1000, and [[Pierre de Fermat|Pierre de Fermat]] employed it in number theory in the 17th century.

Subfield of mathematics that studies logic through formal systems defining rules of reasoning and their axioms. Its major subareas are model theory, proof theory, set theory and [[Computability theory|recursion theory]]. Research addresses the expressive and deductive power of formal systems and the foundations of mathematics. The field emerged in the mid-19th century, and in the early 20th century [[David Hilbert|David Hilbert]] proposed a program to prove the consistency of mathematics. Results of [[Kurt Gödel|Kurt Gödel]] and Gerhard Gentzen provided only partial resolution, but clarified the issues involved. Work in [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory|set theory]] showed that all mathematics can be formalized in terms of sets, and this led to proof assistants such as Lean, which can completely verify difficult theorems.

Study of algorithms for selecting the best element from a set of alternatives, usually by maximizing or minimizing a function. It is divided into discrete optimization, where the sought object is an integer, permutation or graph, and continuous optimization, where it is drawn from a continuous set. The function is called an objective, cost, loss or utility function, and optimal solutions are sought among feasible solutions that satisfy constraints. Because maximizing a function is equivalent to minimizing its negative, the field usually works with minimization. Key techniques include [[Linear programming|linear programming]], [[Nonlinear programming|nonlinear programming]] and [[Gradient descent|gradient descent]], and the field underlies [[Operations research|operations research]], [[Economics|economics]] and [[Machine learning|machine learning]].

Rectangular array of numbers or other mathematical objects arranged in rows and columns. A matrix with m rows and n columns is an m × n matrix, and a matrix with the same number of rows and columns is called square. Matrices are used in [[Linear algebra|linear algebra]] as linear maps, in geometry for transformations such as rotations, and in numerical analysis, where many computational problems are reduced to matrix computations. A square matrix is invertible if and only if its [[Determinant|determinant]] is nonzero. Matrix theory began as a sub-branch of linear algebra but grew to include [[Graph theory|graph theory]], algebra, combinatorics and statistics. The term was coined by James Joseph Sylvester in 1850, and [[Arthur Cayley|Arthur Cayley]] formalized [[Matrix multiplication|matrix multiplication]] in the 1850s.

Binary operation in [[Linear algebra|linear algebra]] that produces a [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] from two matrices. The product of an m × n matrix and an n × p matrix is an m × p matrix, defined only when the number of columns in the first matrix equals the number of rows in the second. Each entry of the product is the [[Dot product|dot product]] of a row of the first matrix and a column of the second. Matrix multiplication is associative but not generally commutative, and it represents the composition of linear maps. It was first described by Jacques Philippe Marie Binet in 1812.

Japanese poet of the [[Edo period|Edo period]], regarded as the greatest master of [[Haiku|haiku]]. Born Matsuo Kinsaku in Iga Province, he served as a page to Tōdō Yoshitada, with whom he shared a love of *haikai no renga*, a form of collaborative linked verse. He left that service after Yoshitada's death in 1666 and settled in Edo, where he taught and edited anthologies. Haiku was then called hokku, the opening verse of a renga sequence, and he refined it into a standalone form that emphasizes seasonal imagery and simple description. From the 1680s he traveled widely across Japan and recorded his journeys in travel essays, of which *Oku no Hosomichi* (*The Narrow Road to the Deep North*) is the best known. He died in Osaka during his final journey.

American actor, screenwriter and producer. Damon co-wrote the screenplay for *Good Will Hunting* (1997) with [[Ben Affleck|Ben Affleck]], and the two won the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Original Screenplay. He became a leading man in the *Bourne* films and the *Ocean's* trilogy. He won a Golden Globe Award for Best Actor for playing an astronaut stranded on [[Mars|Mars]] in *The Martian* (2015). He was nominated for a Primetime Emmy Award for the HBO biopic *Behind the Candelabra* (2013). Damon co-founded the nonprofit Water.org in 2009 with engineer Gary White, which promotes market-based financing for safe water and sanitation.

American cartoonist, creator of *The Simpsons* and *Futurama*. His comic strip *Life in Hell* (1977–2012) was carried in 250 weekly newspapers at its peak. Animated shorts he made for *The Tracey Ullman Show* became *The Simpsons*, the longest-running American primetime television series. He co-developed *Futurama* with David X. Cohen and created *Disenchantment* for [[Netflix|Netflix]]. He has won 14 Primetime Emmy Awards and received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame|Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 2012.
